utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Perhaps we should check that everyone can hear? Can you hear me on the English channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hodak, can you hear me? Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can everyone hear? Can the accused hear? The Registrar has the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-T, the Court against General Blaskic, and this is a hearing for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this is a request for provisional release that was presented yesterday by the Defence, Who is seated at the Prosecutor's bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear for the Prosecution. I am assisted at the Bar table with Miss Payman,

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who is representing General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Blaskic is represented by attomeys at law Zvonimir Hodak and my colleague, Mrs. Nela Pedisic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is a request for provisional release under Rule 65 and, therefore, although it is not compulsory, our Rules require that we hear the host country, in other words, the representatives of the Dutch government which we have called. Are they present? Are they going to be taking the floor? Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, sir, right after the hearing yesterday, we contacted the Foreign Affairs Ministry of the Netherlands, and this morning we received the following answer that I shall read to you The host 'Country is not able to appear today given the very short time span that was given. The person from the Ministry who would have appeared is abroad, and the host country would request a written request in the future. This was not the case since because of the very short time span we called on the phone. Therefore, in the future they are requesting to be informed in writing and they would also like to be informed in writing of the questions that are to be put to the authorities. Therefore, unfortunately, I was not able to fulfill the task that you requested from me yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you to the Registrar, We shall withdraw to determine what we should do because of the absence of the host country. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: After having heard what our Registrar has read about the position of the host country, the Tribunal will now continue the hearing for the request for provisional release, and what happened this morning will be included in the request. We will interpret the question, rather, the answer from the host country and it will be interpreted as it should be, or it should be interpreted without the need for hearing the host country. The Tribunal would, however, like to criticize that attitude. It is difficult to understand that there is not a single legal specialist within the Ministry of Justice or of Defense at the Netherlands who could come here, and to say we have to inform in advance in order to have somebody appear as a person called to the Tribunal as provided for in Rule 65. The Tribunal says that it will, therefore, interpret the answer from the Registrar, as it was transmitted quickly, it will interpret the request as it wants because no delays can be accepted, There is, of course, a reasonable delay which can be accepted to allow a lawyer who is coming from far away or when the Office of the Prosecutor needs time to be organized. We are not closed minded when it comes to all different types of consideration, but when asking for provisional release for somebody who is incarcerated, it has to take place in the quickest manner possible. Since the host country is the host country here, it does seem to be an institution which might be something which we could mobilize immediately. It could be a civil service from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Justice. Of course, the Tribunal will, therefore, interpret the answer which will be attached to the case file, the answer from the Ministry, and it will be part of the answer. We are now giving the floor to Mr. Hodak to present the request for provisional release for General Blaskic, but first, if you do not mind, I would like to ask General Blaskic to tell us whether he has any observations to make about what has just taken place; if not, we will immediately give the floor to Mr. Hodak. Do you wish to speak, General Blaskic? THE ACCUSED GENERAL BLASKIC [Original in Serbo-Croat]: No, your Honour, I have nothing to say to this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear that. I did not get the interpretation of that. Am I supposed to change buttons, change channels? Thank you. I am sorry, 1 again made a technical error here. Under these conditions, the request for provisional release as presented by Mr. Hodak or by his colleague, we can now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, yesterday I briefly elaborated my position and the position of my client in respect of the application of Rule 65(A), (B) and (C). As you may know, yesterday we were given one part of evidence by the Prosecutor after a considerable time, and we had a chance to read this evidence. We know that the quality of evidence will be decided on by the Chamber and that the Defence cannot speak about the quality of evidence, but I have to say that the evidence that we received yesterday from legal point of view are irrelevant. It is a kind of evidence which, for example, speaks about the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna which is a political act in which my client did not take any part and, even if he had, this is not something that he can be charged with. All I want to say that in respect of relevant evidence, competent evidence, on which the decision can be based, we have not made any significant progress from 2nd April when Mr. Blaskic entered his plea of innocence. As you know, General Blaskic appeared before this Tribunal voluntarily. He was not arrested. He was not arrested in Germany, France or Austria, but he arrived in The Hague on a commercial flight and made himself available to this Tribunal and this Trial Chamber. This proves that General Blaskic is not the kind of person which would abuse your goodwill in case he is provisionally released in accordance with Article 65, What we have stressed several times, and what we try to present clearly in our talks with the Prosecution before the arrival of General Blaskic to The Hague, is that the Croatian government will give written guarantees that General Blaskic will always appear before this Tribunal at the exact time whenever the Tribunal so requests, that is to say, at all hearings. Why can the Croatian government guarantee for General Blaskic? Simply because General Blaskic is an active member, active officer, of the Croatian Army. He is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence which is under the Croatian government. As an officer of the Croatian Army, General Blaskic is bound to obey all the orders issued to him by the Ministry of Defence and the government of Croatia. This is the reason why I can claim, why I can maintain, that the Croatian government is prepared to give all the necessary guarantees to this Trial Chamber, that the accused General Blaskic will always appear before this Trial Chamber whenever so requested by it. A further reason which speaks in favor to what we suggested yesterday and what we are elaborating today is the law of the Republic of Croatia which has been recently passed on the co-operation of the Republic of Croatia with the International Tribunal in The Hague. It is a constitutional law and it was passed, voted, by the Croatian parliament with two-thirds, with only one vote against and four votes abstained. So, a great majority of the Croatian parliament voted in favor of that constitutional act which commits, obliges, the Republic of Croatia to respect, to abide by, all requests of the International Tribunal, therefore, all the requests of this Trial Chamber and you, -Mr. President. So, each of your requests is a legal obligation of the Republic of Croatia and he Republic of Croatia is bound to respect its constitutional laws. So, from the legal point of view, General Blaskic should appear before this Tribunal whenever so requested and the government should give guarantees for that. Yesterday I said that General Blaskic is prepared to observe all conditions that may be imposed by this Trial Chamber, that is, all restrictions that the trial in its decision would set out. Therefore, General Blaskic declares through myself, Defence counsel, that he will observe those conditions and he will not default on it if this Trial Chamber trusts him. I would like to add something which may not be as relevant from the legal point of view but may be served as some sort of guidance for this Trial Chamber in reaching the decision this case; this is the personal family situation of General Blaskic which is at the same time very difficult and tragic. Yesterday we heard this story and we can prove that in a very short amount of time we can give names of 25 relatives of General Blaskic who have been killed in this war, including his father, Ivan, who was killed in the very area mentioned in the indictment. In addition to his father, 24 relatives of General Blaskic were also killed. We have evidence to prove this and we can make this evidence available to the Tribunal and the Prosecution as soon as possible. Furthermore, General Blaskic cares for his mother after the death of his father, his wife who is also unemployed, his son, his eight year old son, and his one month old son too. I here dispose of written documents proving that the wife of General Blaskic is currently in hospital. She is very seriously ill and she is being treated. His children, therefore, are being, taken care of by his friends which, you would admit, is not a normal situation, that although the parents are living, children have to be in somebody else's custody, children as young as one month. The last piece of evidence which I would like to talk about today, Mr. President, is something that I did not mention yesterday because I did not know all the relevant details. We spoke with the Prosecutor several times and the Prosecutor knows he was present at those talks, and we told him that until the constitutional law of the Republic of Croatia on the co-operation with the Tribunal in The Hague is not passed, we are willing to help General Blaskic arrive at the Hague voluntarily, but we wanted for this certain privileges which is perfectly normal in the talks between Prosecution and Defence. We requested that General Blaskic be granted certain privileges, that is, to have better conditions that he would have in a normal detention. We requested that he be accommodated outside the detention unit and that he be allowed to communicate with his wife by telephone, and that he also be enabled to have some physical exercise and other things which are normally available in a usual residence as opposed to the detention unit of the United Nations. On I7th April, President Cassese met all our requests in his decision and in which he stated an old Latin Rule which we translate "in dubio pro reo" , which says that in case of doubt the Tribunal needs to be either lenient or rule in favour of the accused. President Cassese made us, therefore, intimated, that there are certain doubts that General Blaskic is actually a war criminal and that he committed the crimes alleged in the indictment. So he showed certain goodwill and allowed for some privileges to be granted to General Blaskic and reached a decision according to which General Blaskic would be allowed, is allowed, to live in a house with three rooms from which he could telephone to his wife and in which he could prepare his defence and meet -- he was also enabled to meet with his counsel and his wife outside that house in an hotel and he also had the right to spend a night with his wife, with his family, in an hotel once a month. We were satisfied with the privileges that were granted to him by the President Cassese. However, yesterday we learned from the Registrar and Mr. Marro that, unfortunately, the Tribunal, that is the Registry, cannot implement what President Cassese granted to General Blaskic in his decision of 17th April. Legal and other obstacles that appeared in the implementation of the decision actually prevent the realization of what has been granted to General Blaskic. The decision has been forwarded to New York and it is going to be discussed by legal advisers of the Secretary General. I do not know and I am not an optimist in respect of what they are going, to decide, because this is something which can be implemented at a practical level here only in The Hague. Therefore, we are in this strange position. We have disclosed the names of witnesses to the Prosecutor. We have appeared voluntarily in The Hague, but yesterday we were notified that in spite of the goodwill of President Cassese there is going to be nothing; it was all to no avail. I, therefore, think that this could be also one of the reasons that this Trial Chamber can take into consideration, namely, to take into consideration all the facts that I have mentioned here, If General Blaskic had, indeed, committed all the crimes alleged in the indictment, he would have never surrendered voluntarily to The Hague. We know that he is the only person from the former Yugoslavia who has come voluntarily. If this had not coincided with the birth of his son, he would have done it earlier. The Prosecution knows that I explained several times to the Tribunal that they simply must take into consideration his personal situation, namely, the birth of his son, Once this was over and once General Blaskic came to my office, he told me: "You can now notify the Tribunal that I will come voluntarily. I am innocent. I am a professional soldier. I have graduated from a military academy and I have always been the first in my generation, the best student in my generation. Considering what we have here in relation to war crimes, I am certainly the last person that should be here. I am the person who abided by the Geneva Conventions in the most strict manner". I have at my disposal between 10 and 15 orders issued by him by which those who committed war crimes were severely punished. I will not take any of your precious time. I have explained all the reasons, all the circumstances, that I believe to be relevant. I would like you to know that we have not received any of the promises; any of the promises as for his house arrest, not a single promise has been really now fulfilled and General Blaskic does not have anything of what has been promised to him in respect to his accommodation here. I appeal to you to trust General Blaskic. He is prepared to observe all conditions imposed by this Trial Chamber and he is not going to default on his promise. We promise that it is possible here to have a trial of an officer, and this can also be under the conditions which are normal for any other trials.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One moment. (The learned Judges conferred)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With the agreement of my colleagues and before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I would first like to give the floor to the Registrar. It has been explained to the Tribunal what the current situation is concerning General Blaskic’s detention. Turning to the Registrar, could you tell us where we are as regards the detention.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, and your Honours, I am unfortunately, in a position where I must confirm what Mr. Hodak has said. The legal situation is as follows. President Cassese, in two orders pursuant to Rule 64 of the Rules dealing with the modification of detention conditions ordered the registry to set up new arrangements for General Blaskic’s detention. Unfortunately, the legal specialists in my office and myself realised that there were legal obstacles and problems which had not been noted by anybody to that point, and that those problems created many difficulties for us to implement the instructions which we had ,received from president Cassese. I will not go into all the details unless you ask me to. We contacted the headquarters in New York to receive approval. I am not hopeless or completely pessimistic about getting an answer, but I cannot make a promise at this point. The Registry was brought into this very, very, recently, and it was not involved in this from the very beginning. In any case, I am not able to execute President Cassese’s order. Mrs. Sampayo, the Registrar, informed the President the day before yesterday of this in writing, and we have given a copy of this letter both to the Defence and to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning again to the Registrar, could you, however, tell the Tribunal, even approximately without revealing anything that has to do with your competence, but what type of legal obstacles are involved and what are you asking New York to approve? Excuse me for asking you this question, but it would throw light on the work of the Tribunal because the issue is, apparently, a complex one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will go into some of the details then. The problem is twofold. The practical execution of the decision from President Cassese does, in fact, indicate that we must have co-operation with the host country, that is, the government of the Netherlands. The law in this country, that is the Netherlands. apparently, does not permit the Dutch authorities under any conditions to participate in being involved in the detention of someone who has been held by another jurisdiction which is not the one of the Netherlands. Therefore, the Dutch authorities who about this subject have shown that they were willing to co-operate are coming up against a legal obstacle which was not foreseen. On the other hand, the Tribunal and the Registry are unable to have the authority concerning a different place of detention which is not connected with the United Nations, and the Registry has no authority over personnel which is not UN personnel, We can do this if we are competent and can give instructions to make sure that follow up is ensured for the detention. This is the request that we made to headquarters. I am not sure that this situation is a simple one, since there are also financial constraints which come into play here with the other problems that I have just mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can take the risk of saying that possibly -- this is for sure in any case -- the powers according to which the President modified the detention conditions stem from Rule 64, and the Tribunal must not make a mistake in its interpretation saying that right now we are working within the framework of detention.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: General Blaskic is a detained person, not only is he a detained personpursuant to Rule 64, as you have just pointed out, but I can also say de facto, except for one night, he has always slept at the detention unit of the United Nations here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is really very difficult for a court to give the impression, to make people think, that it has to rule depending on various obstacles which are before it. I can only deplore this fact, as I have pointed out. However, given this fact I must say that the Tribunal does not want to rule on a request for provisional release depending only on this or that consideration, whether it be financial or having to do with legal obstacles which might be legitimate, obstacles which the host country has raised. I would, however, perhaps like the Prosecution, to whom I will give the floor, to explain in his introduction, because he is really the only party present here who is supposed to know the origin of these agreements since the Tribunal is not a party to them and, apparently, the Registry is not either. In the end, only the two parties today who are responsible for the fate of the request for provisional release as expressed by Mr. Hodak could say something about these to say that the agreements that were reached were reached outside of the knowledge of the judges. Obviously, the President did not work as a judge but, rather, as the president of the Tribunal. So before going into your conclusions, I will give you the floor. Could you tell us something more about the origin, the type, the content of these agreements and the interpretation you have of them. The situation is an unfortunate one, but I must say about which the Tribunal must not be involved. The provisional release of a detained person who has been charged must be judjed according to the text ruling or goverrning the provisional release. So I now turn to the Prosecutor and ask him to speak, both to develop the conclusions which you would like to develop having to do with the request for provisional release as part of Rule 64 which presented by General Blaskic, Perhaps, first, if you might give us some clarifications about your point of view when it comes to these agreements which, apparently, cannot be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my understanding of the arrangements that were entered into between the Prosecution and the Defence concerning Rule 64 were as follows. It is my understanding, your Honours, that initially the question of bail was broached with the Prosecution, but the prosecution opposed any question of bail I in terms of whether or not we would be agreeable to a submission made by the Defence on the question of bail. It then moved to a consideration of whether or not the conditions of detention could be modified to such an extent that would satisfy the accused coming to The Hague voluntarily. As your Honours know, it is not a matter for the Prosecution at all to have any business with the conditions of detention. That is a matter beyond the competence of he Prosecutor. The only promise that the Prosecutor could make or any agreement that we could enter into would be the attitude that we took before the President, if the Defence thought fit to make an application under Rule 64 to go before the President and ask for a modification of the conditions of detention. If your Honours please, the Prosecutor has fulfilled its promise. It did do that on certain conditions that were agreed between the parties. It went before the President and it agreed. It can do no more. That is the end of the Prosecutor's powers in this. Unfortunately, if this order that has been made by the President cannot be implemented, it does not change the position of the Prosecutor. We still supported that position and we still support it now, but we can do nothing to assist in the implementation of the order other than that because it is totally beyond our competence. Your Honours, I do not know whether it is necessary for me to go into the order that was made by the President -- it is quite an extensive document -- but throughout it raises the issue of involvement of the Netherlands government. Obviously, this was a question that had to be incorporated in this, because otherwise you have a situation where this person is outside of the only facility available in the United Nations to detained people here, namely, the prison at Scheveningen. So, therefore, any other arrangement could only be done with the assistance and co-operation of the host government. My understanding was that initially there was to be an agreement by the host government in respect of the proposals that were made between the parties, but hearing now from the Registrar, it would seem that any arrangements or discussions that, apparently, were had at an early stage have fallen foul of the law of the Netherlands. But, apart from that, there is not much that the Prosecution can do to assist, I regret, because it is a matter beyond our competence. Your Honours, this is an application dealing with provisional release pursuant to Rule 65. If I may, I would like to now turn to that question. Your Honours, the Prosecutor has and is opposed to the grant of provisional release pursuant to Rule 65. Your Honours, it is submitted that Rule 65 raises a presumption of non-release. It is clear that the policy underpinning this presumption results from the grave nature of the offences in the Tribunal's jurisdiction. Your Honours, this is reflected in some jurisdictions where very serious or capital offences, the old form of capital offences, used to exist; in some cases there was no such thing as a right to bail. In respect of some offences, in some jurisdictions there is a presumption of bail, but this is the complete reverse, in our submission, in relation to the Tribunal. We say that this is so because of the very serious nature of the crimes, In our submission, your Honours, the severity of the accused's charges is clear from the indictment and his, the accused's, involvement in the killing of over 100 civilians, including women and children, in the Lasva Valley area between 16th and 20th April 1993 as part of a plan to systematically removed Bosnian Muslim civilians from central Bosnia. This, in our submission, highlights the seriousness of the accused's crimes. Your Honours, the provision of Rule 65 uses the term "exceptional circumstances". In our submissions, "exceptional circumstances" contemplate an unusual or rare occurrence. Accordingly, the circumstances giving rise to the Defence request must be uncommon or of a very rare nature, Your Honours, when dealing with applications of this kind, in most jurisdictions it is common to look at the number of elements, a number of the issues, that are raised by a bail application. Firstly, courts traditionally look at the nature of the offence. In domestic jurisdictions, both civil and common law, the less serious the offence, the more likely an accused will be provisionally released pending the trial. However, this Tribunal's jurisdiction relates to the most serious crimes known to the criminal calendar. The accused, amongst other charges, is charged with being individually responsible and in his capacity as a superior for the acts of his subordinates in the wounding, murder, deportation and maltreatment of civilians. In our submission, it is plain that the nature of offences are extremely serious. Therefore, in our submission, the nature of the offence does not give rise to exceptional circumstances whereby provisional release should be considered. Another consideration that courts frequently look to is what was the role played by the accused in a crime? The question of whether or not the bail is granted can depend upon the role played. The greater the role in the crime, the less likely the application for bail could succeed, The accused has been charged as being a participant in the execution of war crimes as a superior to the perpetrators committing those crimes. Your Honours, the accused was the commander of the Croatian Defence Council, the Bosnian Croat armed forces in central Bosnia. During this period he was responsible through his subordinates, military and paramilitary, for the persecution of Bosnian Muslims throughout the Lasva Valley area. The evidence is clear that the Croatian Defence Council, military and paramilitary, were participants causing the death, wounding, deportation imprisonment and destruction of the entire Bosnian Muslim community in that area. Significantly, the accused was present in Lasva Valley when the attacks were occurring. Therefore, this factor, the role of the accused, in our submission, should not be considered as an exceptional circumstance justifying his release on bail. Your Honours, the issue of the quality of the evidence has been raised. As can be seen from the indictment, the charges against the accused are considerable. In our submission, it is a strong case. High ranking officials from the United Nations Protection Forces, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to military orders from the accused, provide, in our submission, excellent evidence that the accused had full command over the HVO in central Bosnia when and where these atrocities were committed. Numerous statements will provide evidence that it was the HVO military and paramilitary who were involved in, amongst other activities, the massacre of at least 100 civilians between 16th and 20th April 1993. Significantly, if your Honours please, the night before the Lasva Valley massacre occurred on 16th April 1993, a co-accused, Dario Kordic, appeared with the accused on television where Kordic said: "My soldiers are ready, only waiting for orders." At 5.30 a.m. the following morning, the murders, woundings, detention and destruction of Bosnian Muslim and Muslim property commenced by the HVO simultaneously across the valley in nine separate villages, all within 30 kilometers, whilst the accused was present in the middle of the Lasva Valley. A United Nations Protection Force witness from the Lasva Valley area conclude that the attacks were well planned, and that they would take at least several weeks to plan. The evidence against the accused has come from numerous sources thereby providing a great degree of reliability. Therefore, in our submission, the quality of the evidence is of such a high calibre that it is not an exceptional circumstance within the meaning of the Rule. Further in our submission, your Honours, we have not heard of any great substance from the Defence as to their argument on the quality of the evidence. Although the Prosecution carries the burden of proving the guilt of he accused (and it will discharge that burden) in relation to this particular motion, it is their motion, If they wish to assert that there are exceptional circumstances, then it must fall to them, in our submission, to convince you that there are exceptional circumstances. In our submission, they have ailed in their task. The accused has raised on a number of occasions the question of the length of time awaiting the trial. In our submission, your Honors, the general rule ordinarily applied in relation to this, is that if the likely penalty is commensurate or far outweighs the likely time a detained accused would await his or her trial, then there is a greater likelihood that he or she would be released. This practice is an attempt to avoid serving sentences in excess of what reflects the true culpability. If this accused is found guilty to the full extent of the charges, it is submitted that an extensive period of imprisonment would be served. Your Honours, in terms of dealing with this question of length of time, it is difficult, just upon a reading of the Rules, to have any clear idea of what is a reasonable time to be detained in custody pending the commencement of the trial. I referred yesterday, your Honours, to Rule 73 (B) which, at least in an indirect way, contemplates that a period of 60 days would not be excessive because that is the period of time that is allowed for the Defence to bring motions. Another issue, if your Honours please, that I think is relevant and, in my submission, gives some assistance in determining this question of any delay, relates to the vast gulf that appears between the test to be applied in the submission of the indictment under Rule 47(A), the reasonable grounds for believing test, and the ultimate test under Rule 87 of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. In our submission, your Honours, there must be a period of time contemplated when the Prosecution would move from its position at the time of submission of the indictment for confirmation to the time when the trial commences. Similar provisions apply in numerous jurisdictions in Europe, and in the short time that I have had available to me, if your Honours please, and I profess to have no expertise as in such matters, but I understand that in Italy the position with respect to the maximum length of preventative measures before the trial starts, according to the law of ltaly, it is one year for crimes punishable with detention over 20 years or with life sentences. So, under the law of Italy, a period of one year is contemplated as a period of detention prior to trial in relation to those offences. In relation to lesser offences, for example crimes punishable detention riot less than six years the period is three months. So, your Honours, this is an operation of that particular Rule. The situation in Germany, if your Honours please, it is a complicated provision but it generally relates to a period of six months for serious crime and then there is provision in the legislation to allow that to be extended. Your Honours, as 1 understand the position in relation to France, the initial period is a period of four months once the case has been remitted to the judge d'instruction, and further applications can be made for an extension of this period. Where the offence is a grave offence, such as armed robbery, murder, rape, of that nature, they are punishable with sentences for 25 years or life imprisonment. The initial period of remand can be up to a period of one year. I understand, your Honours, there is an opportunity for appeal, but it can be for that period of time. Your Honours, so these are the periods of time ordinarily contemplated in our jurisdictions in Europe, in my submission, which may be of some assistance in determining what is a reasonable time. Another factor, your Honours, is the question of the likelihood of appearing for trial. This is another factor, as I say, that is often considered in applications of this nature, Despite the accused's submission that he attended the Tribunal voluntarily, it is the Prosecution's submission that if the accused was provisionally released, it is highly likely that he would fail to attend at some time prior to judgment being delivered. The maximum penalty the Tribunal can impose for these offences is life imprisonment. It is submitted that these offences will be placed at' the high end of the scale of seriousness and, consequently, would result in a lengthy term of imprisonment if the accused was convicted. If the developments pre and during trial appear less favorable in the accused's mind than he may have envisaged when he volunteered himself to the Tribunal, it is, in our submission, likely that he may flee to avoid any possible lengthy detention, In determining this, it is that the accused has been at large since mid-November 1995 when he would have been aware of the issued indictments and warrants against him. In our submission, this accused, as far as we know, and we have heard nothing from the Defence on this, has no property in this jurisdiction, so he has nothing here to hold him to this jurisdiction. He has no family in this jurisdiction and he has no employment in this jurisdiction. Often courts take such matters into consideration because they consider, well, if the person's family, property and employment are all in the jurisdiction, then it is likely the person may be more inclined to stay. In this case there is none of that. Another factor that is often considered in determining these applications is the likelihood of any danger being imposed to victims or witnesses. At this stage the Prosecution is not aware of any danger from this accused to any victim, witness or other person. However, if released once witnesses become known to the accused, the situation may change. We just cannot be sure of this and, in our submission, we cannot afford to speculate on this Your Honours, also there is another consideration which, in our submission, is relevant. That is that if the witnesses themselves become aware that the accused is at large, then they themselves, in fear, may refuse to eo-operate any further with the Tribunal. In our submission, and we will be seeking from the Tribunal protective measures in relation to witnesses, if those protective measures are granted in relation to witnesses, in our submission, they are far less effective, far less secure, if the accused is at large, because one of the major factors in providing comfort for witnesses is the knowledge of the fact that the accused is in custody and cannot gain access to them. It is regrettable, your Honors, and your Honour has observed this, that we have not heard from the host government in this country, but it is at all possible that the Netherlands government may be reluctant to have indicted war criminals roaming freely in their community. They may say, no,'we are not prepared to permit this and that anyone who is released on bail from the Tribunal must return to Croatia or wherever. If that is the case, in my submission, your Honours, 'then there is absolutely no guarantee whatsoever that this accused will be available and present for trial, particularly if things change, particularly if when he sees the full extent of the Prosecution case he decides that his prospects of acquittal are not quite as good as lie had originally anticipated. Bail could be offered, a bail bond could be offered, but what amount? What amount could be set? In my submission, no amount of money would replace freedom if people have the opportunity to escape. This Tribunal cannot be equated when dealing with issues such as this with a State, a State that has coercive powers to control the entering and exiting of people within and out of its borders, who can search within its community for people who have decided for whatever reason to hide. This Tribunal has no power to do that. It cannot control where people come or go. It cannot do the usual things that States do to keep people within its borders. In my submission, your Honours, once this accused is released into the community so far as the Tribunal's powers are concerned, that is the end of the matter. Finally, your Honours, in due course it is expected that numerous people will be brought before these courts and tried for war crimes. No doubt if bail can be granted and readily granted, and if the meaning of "exceptional circumstances" is not, in our submission, given its full and proper meaning, then more and more applications can be brought and the precedent set by release will be invoked time and time again. If States co-operate with the Tribunal and put considerable resources, effort and money into tracking down and locating war criminals, people who have been indicted by the Tribunal, and they put this effort into surrendering them to the Tribunal and because of the precedent set we just then release them on bail and, as a consequence of that they are released, then I submit, your Honours, that the co-operation and assistance of States may likely fade, because they are not going to put their effort and energy into such activities if we have a practice whereby release on bail becomes an ordinary day occurrence. So, it is for these reasons, if your Honours please, that "exceptional circumstances" means exactly that. It is a very rare and exceptional circumstance. Indeed, it is hard to envisage what exceptional circumstance would justify release. In our submission, the Defence have come nowhere in establishing that in relation to this application: Unless I can assist your Honours with anything further, that is my submission

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. I believe that we are reaching the end of our discussions. Would the Defence or General Blaskic possibly like to say something? Does the Defence have a few comments to make? I will then give the floor back to the Prosecution because at one point there must be absolute bounds between the two parties. Mr. Hodak, would you like to speak again? I would also like to give the floor to General Blaskic and then, of course, at one point I have to close the proceedings. Some brief observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be short, Certain facts do not correspond to the real situation. As the Prosecutor stated, General Blaskic has indeed been indicted for individual criminal responsibility, but he also said that General Blaskic was accused as a perpetrator. I did not find that in the indictment. Although I have read it several times, this is not mentioned anywhere. There is not a single proof that General Blaskic committed any of the crimes alleged in the indictment. The Prosecutor, among other things, states that General Blaskic was commander of the HVO and that other paramilitary groups also committed crimes in the area of central Bosnia, namely the Lasva Valley. Unfortunately, this is not true and I will warn the Prosecutor of that. I will just mention to this Chamber the Dayton Agreement which clearly says that the HVO was the regular army of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, in the Dayton Agreement, according to the Dayton Agreement, a joint command of Muslims and Croats has been established in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In August '95 the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic,appointed joint commanders of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatian Defence Council. Those joint commanders, and we are speaking about August '95, those joint commanders are Rasin Delic and General Tihornir Blaskic. General Tihomir Blaskic is charged with war crimes committed in April 93 and the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina appointed him as a Council, which proves that he Croatian Defence Council was not a paramilitary group but a regular army. As for the objection of the Prosecutor that we did not make any concrete comments on the evidence, I just want to ask him back, when did we have time to make any significant comments on the evidence which was disclosed only yesterday evening? Once again, the evidence is not relevant for this case. As for the special exceptional circumstances, I can just state once again that one of those exceptional circumstances is the voluntary arrival of General Blaskic to The Hague. As for the General Blaskic not having any property in the Netherlands, I would like to say that General Blaskic has already paid 217,000 Dutch guilders to the Dutch Government for the accommodation outside the UN detention unit which has not been implemented, and he has requested to pay 200,000 guilders a month to the Dutch Government for his accommodation. Therefore, General Blaskic has means to finance his stay in the Netherlands. As for the bail, it is a special guarantee that the accused will not abscond in every national system. In this case, the Prosecutor says that, that we cannot think of any amount of money in this case, but we must agree that all national jurisdictions, all legal systems, have this provision of bail. Therefore, I believe that a high amount of bail can be a guarantee that the accused, that the accused would appear before the Tribunal. As for the argument of the Prosecutor that his being at liberty would affect the witnesses, this is not true because all the witnesses that have been contacted so far, they have agreed to appear, they have agreed to give their statements while General Blaskic was at liberty. Therefore, I ask this Tribunal to make a precedent here, to think of reasons of justice and to enable General Blaskic to defend himself while at liberty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, gentlemen, I have nothing special to add except that, once again, I would like to confirm that I have come here voluntarily and that I have made an undertaking to appear before this Tribunal whenever so requested depending on the decision that will be reached here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, you will have to start again. T0 THE ACCUSED: Gentlemen, I do not have anything special to add to this except that I would like to say, once again, that I have come to this Tribunal voluntarily and that I am ready to comply with all the requests of this Trial Chamber,

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No clarifications? No additional comments? I turn to my colleagues now to ask if they have any questions they would like to ask. Mr. Prosecutor would you like to add something now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honours, I did not receive the translation. There is one matter I would like to correct at this stage, and it relates to the question of responsibility and which I raised in my submissions, All I wish to do is to refer the Chamber to Count 1 in particular and following of tile indictment where there are references to Articles 7(l) and 7(3) of the Statute. lt. was upon those provisions I was relying when I made my submissions about responsibility. Thank you,

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would the Defence like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: No, thank you,

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. I will now tell you that the Chamber will render its decision this afternoon at 5 o'clock. I will take advantage of this moment to tell you that we will see one another once again for this status conference on preliminary motions following the communication of documents from the Prosecutor and, of course, asking the Prosecutor to submit them as quickly as possible pursuant to Rule 65, 6 and 7, that is all documents he has except for the request he made and to which we will give an answer at the proper time. We have decided we will see one another again on 28th May, the 28th May, let me repeat. I do not know what day of week that is -- it is Tuesday 28th. On that date I would like to have on our calendar all the people here and I would like to ask Mr. Hodak if he would prefer to have it in the mornings or in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not quite understand you. It was first 28th and 27th. Which is the date 28th or 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, 28th. What I am asking you is that it is not important for the Tribunal whether it be in the morning or in the afternoon, The Prosecutor is here. You can come here with your colleague. You are coming from quite a distance. Would you prefer it to be in the morning, or in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if possible the afternoon would suit us better for technical reasons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to call the attention of he Tribunal to the fact that the courtroom will be being used by the Tadic case, so I think maybe 5 or 5.30 would be good for the interpretation problems.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have recalled very politely right now what you said yesterday. In fact I should have remembered. So it will be in the afternoon. Would 5.30 be all right for you? 5.15? MR. HODAK- Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Tuesday, 28th May at 5.15 for the status conference, answer to the request that was made yesterday by the Prosecutor which I hope in the meantime will have been able to have checked everything that he has said he would check on yesterday. In the meantime he will have already given all of the documents that are not covered by other Rules to the Defence, so that on 28th it can say on 28th whether it does intend to raise any preliminary motions. At that point the Tribunal will decide how long after that, 60 days afterwards, whether it wail need 60 days in order to present their preliminary motions, if there are any. In the meantime having to do with provisional release, Trial Chamber will render its decision this afternoon at 5 o'clock. The court stands adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned for a short time)
